title: The Ophites are no Christians
source_text: Τοιοῦτόν τι δή μοι φαίνεται ὁ Κέλσος οἰκονομῶν ἐκτεθεῖσθαι, ὡς ἄρα Χριστιανοὶ λέγουσι κατηραμένον θεὸν τὸν δημιουργὸν, ἵν᾿ ὁ πιστεύων αὐτῷ ταῦτα καθ᾿ ἡμῶν λέγοντι εἰ δυνατὸν καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ αἱρεῖν ὁρμήσαι Χριστιανοὺς ὡς πάντων ἀσεβεστάτους. φύρων δὲ τὰ πράγματα καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν ἐκτίθεται τοῦ κατηραμένον λέγεσθαι τὸν τῆς κατὰ Μωϋσέα κοσμοποιΐας θεὸν φάσκων ὅτι τοιοῦτός ἐστιν καὶ ἀρᾶς ἄξιος κατὰ τοὺς ταῦτα περὶ αὐτοῦ δοξάζοντας, ἐπείπερ τῷ ὄφει, γνῶσιν καλοῦ καὶ κακοῦ τοῖς πρώτοις ἀνθρώποις εἰσηγουμένῳ, κατηράσατο. εἰδέναι δ᾿ αὐτὸν ἐχρῆν ὅτι οἱ τὰ τοῦ ὄφεως ἑλόμενοι ὡς καλῶς τοῖς πρώτοις ἀνθρώποις συμβουλεύσαντος καὶ Τιτᾶνας καὶ Γίγαντας τοὺς μυθικοὺς ὑπερβαλόντες καὶ Ὀφιανοὶ διὰ τοῦτο καλούμενοι τοσοῦτον ἀποδέουσι τοῦ εἶναι Χριστιανοὶ, ὥστ᾿ οὐκ ἔλαττον Κέλσου κατηγορεῖν αὐτοὺς τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ μὴ πρότερον προσίεσθαί τινα ἐπὶ τὸ συνέδριον ἑαυτῶν. ἐὰν μὴ ἀρὰς θῆται κατὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ. ὅρα γοῦν πῶς ἀλογώτατον πεποίηκεν ὁ Κέλσος ἐν τοῖς κατὰ Χριστιανῶν λόγοις παραλαβὼν ὡς Χριστιανοὺς τοὺς μηδ᾿ ἀκούειν θέλοντας τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, κἂν ὅτι σοφός τις ἢ μέτριος τὰ ἤθη ἢ ἄνθρωπός τις ἦν. τί οὖν εἴη ἂν ἠλιθιώτερον ἢ μανικώτερον οὐ μόνον τῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄφεως ὡς ἀρχηγοῦ τῶν καλῶν χρηματίσαι βουληθέντων ἀλλὰ καὶ Κέλσου, νομίσαντος κατὰ Χριστιανῶν εἶναι κατηγορίας τὰς κατὰ τῶν Ὀφιανῶν; πάλαι μὲν οὖν ὁ τὴν εὐτέλειαν ἀγαπήσας φιλόσοφος Ἑλλήνων καὶ παράδειγμα ἐκθεὶς εὐδαίμονος βίου, ὡς οὐ κωλυόμενος εὐδαιμονεῖν ἀπὸ τῆς παντελοῦς ἀκτημοσύνης, Κυνικὸν ἑαυτὸν ἀνηγόρευσεν· οὗτοι δὲ οἱ ἀνόσιοι ἀπὸ τοῦ πολεμιωτάτου ἀνθρώποις ὄφεως καὶ φρικτοτάτου ὡς οὐκ ἄνθρωποι, ὧν ἐχθρός ἐστιν ὄφις, ἀλλ᾿ ὡς ὄφεις σεμνύνονται ἐπὶ τῷ Ὀφιανοὶ καλεῖσθαι, Εὐφράτην τινὰ εἰσηγητὴν τῶν ἀνοσίων αὐχοῦντες λόγων.
pass_a_gloss: Some such thing Celsus seems to me, managing/contriving (οἰκονομέω), to have set out, that Christians say the creator (δημιουργός) is an accursed god, so that the one believing him saying these against us might, if possible, be impelled (ὁρμάω) even to destroy/kill (αἱρέω) Christians as most impious (ἀσεβέστατος) of all. Mixing up (φύρω) the matters he also sets out the cause of the God of the world-making (κοσμοποιΐα) according to Moses being called accursed, saying that he is such and worthy of curse (ἀρά) according to those holding these opinions (δοξάζω) about him, since he cursed (καταράομαι) the serpent (ὄφις) introducing (εἰσηγέομαι) knowledge (γνῶσις) of good and evil to the first humans. He ought to have known that those choosing (αἱρέομαι) the serpent's side as having counselled (συμβουλεύω) the first humans well, and surpassing (ὑπερβάλλω) the mythical (μυθικός) Titans and Giants, and called Ophites (Ὀφιανοί) for this, are so far from (ἀποδέω) being Christians that they accuse Jesus not less than Celsus and do not admit (προσίεμαι) anyone to their assembly (συνέδριον) before, unless he lays curses (ἀρὰς τίθημι) against Jesus. See then how most irrationally (ἀλογώτατα) Celsus has done in his discourses against Christians, taking as Christians those not even willing to hear the name of Jesus, even that he was some wise man (σοφός) or moderate (μέτριος) in character (ἦθος) or some man. What then would be more foolish (ἠλίθιος) or more mad (μανικός) not only than those wishing to be named (χρηματίζω) from the serpent as leader/originator (ἀρχηγός) of good things, but also than Celsus, thinking the accusations against the Ophites to be against Christians? Of old the philosopher of the Greeks who loved frugality (εὐτέλεια) and set out a pattern (παράδειγμα) of happy (εὐδαίμων) life, as not being prevented from being happy by total lack of possessions (ἀκτημοσύνη), proclaimed (ἀναγορεύω) himself Cynic (Κυνικός); but these unholy (ἀνόσιος) from the serpent most hostile (πολεμιώτατος) to humans and most dreadful (φρικτότατος), as not humans, of whom the serpent is enemy (ἐχθρός), but as serpents, pride themselves (σεμνύνομαι) on being called Ophites, boasting (αὐχέω) of a certain Euphrates as introducer (εἰσηγητής) of the unholy teachings.
pass_b_english: Something of this kind, it seems to me, Celsus contrived when he set out that Christians call the Creator an accursed god, so that anyone who believed him when he says these things against us might, if possible, go so far as to put Christians to death as the most impious of all. Confusing the matter, he also sets out the reason why the God of the world’s making according to Moses is called accursed: he says that he is such, and deserving of a curse, in the view of those who hold these opinions about him, since he cursed the serpent that introduced the knowledge of good and evil to the first human beings (Genesis 3:5, 14).

He ought to have known that those who have taken the serpent’s side, as though it gave the first human beings good counsel, who outdo the Titans and Giants of myth, and who for this reason are called Ophites, are so far from being Christians that they accuse Jesus no less than Celsus does, and admit no one to their assembly unless he first pronounces curses against Jesus.

See, then, how utterly irrational Celsus has been, in his discourse against Christians, in treating as Christians people who will not even hear the name of Jesus, not even to hear it said that he was a wise man, or of modest character, or simply a man. What then could be more foolish or more mad, not only than those who chose to take their name from the serpent as the author of good things, but also than Celsus, who thought that the charges against the Ophites were charges against Christians?

Long ago the philosopher of the Greeks who loved plain living, and who set out a pattern of the happy life, showing that utter lack of possessions did not prevent him from being happy, proclaimed himself a Cynic. But these unholy men pride themselves on being called Ophites, after the serpent, the creature most hostile and most dreadful to human beings, as though they were not human beings, to whom the serpent is an enemy (Genesis 3:15), but serpents; and they boast of a certain Euphrates as the founder of their unholy teachings.

choices.choice: Celsus’s reason for the ‘accursed god’ is given in indirect speech (φάσκων ὅτι), so it is not put in quotation marks. Genesis 3:5 (knowing good and evil, the serpent’s promise) and 3:14 (God’s curse on the serpent). ‘To whom the serpent is an enemy’ is a clear allusion to the enmity of Genesis 3:15. The staged text puts a full stop before ἐὰν μὴ ἀρὰς θῆται; it is one sentence (‘admit no one ... unless he first pronounces curses’). The cursing of Jesus may recall 1 Corinthians 12:3 (‘Jesus is accursed’), but Origen does not quote it; left uncited. αἱρεῖν rendered ‘put to death’ (the usual sense with persons; ‘destroy’ also possible). The Greek philosopher is not named: Diogenes of Sinope, or possibly Antisthenes; the point of the comparison is that ‘Cynic’ comes from ‘dog’ (κύων), as ‘Ophite’ comes from ‘serpent’ (ὄφις); this pun is not spelled out in the reading text because Origen does not spell it out. ‘What could be more foolish or more mad’ anticipates Celsus’s own words, quoted in 6.29.
ὁρμήσαι is active: 'be driven even to' changed to 'go so far as to'
removed added verb 'grant': now 'not even to hear it said that he was ...'; ἄνθρωπός τις rendered 'simply a man'
